title: Quartet Integra’s Debut Album!
content_blocks: I am thrilled to share that Quartet Integra’s debut album has just been released on Yarlung Records!  Kyoka Misawa (Violin I), Rintaro Kikuno (Violin II), Itsuki Yamamoto (Viola), and Ye Un Park (Cello) make up this extraordinarily-talented young quartet, three of whom have known knew each other and played together since they formed in high school in 2015.  The Quartet has completed their three-year residency at the Colburn School and are now based in Hanover, Germany.

Quartet Integra’s debut album on Yarlung Records, which was released today, features Beethoven Op.135 (his last work), Ligeti’s String Quartet No.2, and my own Green Mountains, Now Black. This piece was commissioned by Donna Morton and Coretet for Quartet Integra, and took inspiration from the works of Monteverdi, excerpting passages from Monteverdi’s Orfeo and L’incoronazione di Poppea.

The name Monteverdi means green mountain. I was working on this piece just as the Los Angeles fires were burning, though, making for a marked contrast with such “green mountain” music, until I realized that the mournfulness found in so much of Monteverdi’s music reflected the situation at hand. This is especially true of “Non Morir” (“Don’t Die!”) and “A Dio, Roma” (“Goodbye, Rome”) from Poppea, but could also be said of “Possente Spirto” (“Mighty Spirit”) from Orfeo, in which Orpheus in the netherworld begs to bring his dead wife back to the world of the living.

The one excerpt that does not fit this mournful mold is “Pur Ti Miro” (“I Gaze Upon You”). This love duet at the end of Poppea celebrates the culmination of Poppea’s and Nero’s scheming to divorce and depose Octavia, Nero’s wife, and install Poppea in her stead. In Green Mountains, Now Black the displacement of Octavia by Poppea is rectified by the incorporation of “A Dio Roma,” played simultaneously with and ultimately displacing the joy of “Pur Ti Miro,” as we bid a sad farewell to portions of our beloved city.

On another level, the composition really is “about” the string quartet, and different ways to use the ensemble and the instruments to express mournfulness. One of the first instances of this can be found in the first movement: I realized that Monteverdi’s operatic styling—with choked voices, chromatic inflections, and stuttering sobs—can be mirrored by the stylized sobs found in Klezmer “krekhts”—literally cracks, but describing the exact same sort of choked voices and stuttering sobs. I also exploited different playing techniques to portray how a seemingly placid surface can disguise seething turmoil just under that surface. This takes the form of faster and faster runs in the first movement, which gradually transform into glissandi, creating intertwining melodies similar to what Tchaikovsky did in the last movement of his Symphony No.6.

In the second movement, this turmoil takes the form of arpeggiated chords and tense sustained three-note chords in single instruments.  In the last movement, the bitonal overlay of the two contrasting arias creates the tension.  “A Dio Roma” first appears in the cello, joined by the viola, and then the second violin.  By the end, the first violin—voicing Poppea’s disconcertingly happy vocal line (it ends the opera on a seemingly happy note, but the viewer knows what tragedies have already occurred and are in store)—is left alone.

All of this tragedy and sorrow reflects the feelings of so many of us in Los Angeles, devastated by the Pacific Palisades and Altadena fires.  The members of Quartet Integra understood the contrasting emotions of this piece perfectly, and gave stunning performances.  The recording on the Yarlung CD was completed in a single take!
